slides: Academic writing.
What it is exactly, how it's different from other kinds of writing... and how to make your essay fit it.
Let's start by explaining what academic writing is.
The simple, basic definition is, academic writing is writing whose goal is to present ideas in an organized, clear way.
And like we said in the first lesson, it's the writing you'll use at university. Research, papers, articles.
So we don't just talk in the air, let's compare academic writing with a kind you probably do know. Literary writing.
Literary writing is how stories and books are written. Novels, novellas, the texts you studied in literature classes, or books you've read.
I believe, and I hope, that names like Agnon, Dostoevsky, even J. K. Rowling sound familiar. That's literary writing.
So what are the differences? Let's start with the goal.
In literary writing, the writer wants to share his world with the reader. Maybe through a story about other people, or about himself... but either way, he's sharing his inner world.
Academic writing has one goal, and it has nothing to do with the writer's inner world. We need to explain an idea clearly.
And the explanation is usually made of arguments and facts.
And because of that goal, in literary writing the writer uses a personal tone a lot, and examples from his own life.
There, that's welcome and expected.
Academic writing is more objective. A personal tone is really, really not okay.
Look at this one. High school, my neighbourhood, how I felt. That's a personal story, not an argument.
And here's the same idea in an academic style. Nobody's life story. Just the idea, and why it would happen.
You could say that good academic writing takes the writer out of the text.
When someone reads an academic text, we, the writers, aren't really there.
Think for a moment about a blog you read, or an opinion column in a newspaper. Like a columnist who writes every week.
When you read what he writes, you kind of hear his voice in the background. You imagine him talking.
In academic writing it's not like that. I read the text and I hear... nothing. Just some neutral narrator, or myself.
Think of the reading comprehension passages in the exam. That's academic writing.
When you read them, do you hear someone reading to you? No. Some anonymous narrator reads the text to you.
And if that's the case, it means whoever wrote that text did a good job.
So the language should be like classic news reports. Not opinion columns and blogs. The news reports of the old days.
The narrator's voice is neutral. Formal, respectful, clear, and as factual as possible.
Now, creativity. In literary writing it's welcome and expected. In academic writing it can hurt you.
That doesn't mean creativity is forbidden. But it can hurt you if you don't know how to use it properly.
The writing has to stay inside the borders of the topic you're dealing with. You don't make things up, you don't give back stories.
The writing should be really focused on the topic.
And we don't make up new things to get a great score. If you make up a new expression, that can be fine in literary writing.
In a novel, or a comedy script, someone makes up a phrase and suddenly it's part of the language.
In academic writing, it's not fine at all. A strange expression you make up probably won't become part of anyone's vocabulary. It'll just hurt your score.
Though, I can tell you, as essay raters we sometimes see amazing creativity. Expressions we actually take with us.
Like one student who wrote, in my prevalent opinion. We still smile about it. But it didn't help his score.
Now, appealing to emotion. In literary writing that's legit. Welcome, and expected.
Some would say a good author is one who plays on your heartstrings, and stirs up feelings.
In academic writing, that's not okay at all. The writer has to explain things with logic... by appealing to the mind, not the heart.
Emotional appeals are really common in speeches, by the way. Those fiery speeches that get the crowd all worked up.
Heartbreaking, innocent, watched like criminals. That's trying to make the reader feel something.
And here's the same concern, explained. Stay focused, and to the point.
Taking the writer's personal life out of the text also shows in the grammatical person you use.
In literary writing there's no limit. I, you, he, she, we, they.
In academic writing, the writer can use 'I'... but only in phrases like 'in my opinion' or 'I believe that'. Other than that, no 'I'.
'We' isn't okay. Like, 'we must do this and that'. And 'you', no. We don't talk to the reader. 'So you should...', 'you can see that...'.
Third person is fine. I can talk about 'they'. People, the population, society, and so on.
So look here. We, and you. The writer talks to the reader, and speaks for everyone.
Now, flowery or poetic language. Decorated language, like in poetry.
Of course it's fine in literary writing, but it's not okay in academic writing. The language has to be precise, not decorated.
Silent guardian, sleeping city, shining beacon. Beautiful, maybe. But what is it actually saying?
This is what it was trying to say. Plain, precise... and it has a real reason in it.
Rhetorical devices, and proverbs.
First, rhetorical devices. Those are tools a writer uses to persuade through emotion.
One of the best known is the rhetorical question. A question where the answer is obvious, so you don't really need to ask it.
Picture a speaker on a stage in the city square, talking about workers' conditions. What would we expect from him? Dramatic questions.
The answer's obvious. It's not acceptable. His goal is to fire up the people listening. That's an appeal to emotion, and it's not okay in academic writing.
In the essay, turn the question into a statement... and explain it.
Proverbs are short sayings of life wisdom. Like, a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
In literary writing that's fine, no limit. In academic writing, it's less okay.
Just say what the proverb means, in your own plain words.
In English there's one more thing to watch. Spoken, everyday English. We talk one way, and we write the essay another way.
No contractions. Write 'do not', 'it is', 'cannot'.
No slang, and no chatty words. Children, not kids. Many, not a lot of. And say what the 'stuff' actually is.
And where there's a formal verb, use it. Reduce, not cut down on. Improve, not get better.
And no spoken fillers. Well, basically, let's be honest, like, you know.
Another difference is how strongly you say things.
In literary writing you can be as absolute as you want. No problem.
In academic writing, the writing has to be qualified. We avoid absolute words and extreme positions.
Even when we choose a position, we do it in qualified language. Knowing that the issue has several sides.
The other side probably has some advantages too... or my side has some disadvantages.
None of us is completely right, so we need to be qualified. And we'll see exactly how in the next lesson.
Okay, let's see it all together. Here's a paragraph written in a spoken, personal, emotional style.
Let's be honest, I know I don't, a total nightmare, everyone knows, you'd have to be crazy. A rhetorical question, contractions, 'you', emotion, an absolute claim.
Every one of those is something we just learned to avoid.
And here's the academic version. The same position, against the cameras. But calm, qualified, and explained.
And notice... the position didn't get weaker. It got more convincing.
So let's sum it up quickly. To write in a way that fits academic writing...
Qualified writing is really, really important, and it keeps coming back. We'll come back to it lots of times in the next lessons.
The tone of the writing should be moderate, respectful, calm.
When two people argue, each one shouts at the other. Don't picture that. Picture two people having a debate... who talk quietly to each other.
Each one respects the other side, lets him speak, listens to him.
We need to accept that there's logic on the other side too. Nobody owns the truth, or what's right.
That's the heart of academic writing. That's how we write in a way that fits it.
